findings.claim: The minuet and trio “originated as a stately dance in the Classical era (c.1750–1820)”.
findings.truth: The minuet is a French court dance of the 1600s (Baroque). Classical composers turned it into a standard symphony movement from c.1750. The same lesson already lists the minuet among Baroque dances written in binary form, so the page contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Minuet (French origin, 17th century; standardised as the third movement of Classical symphonies); spec p.5 places binary, ternary and minuet and trio in Baroque, Classical and Romantic music

findings.claim: “What letter pattern represents binary form?” offers both AB (keyed correct) and AABB.
findings.truth: The lesson twice states that AABB is still binary form, so a student who learned the lesson could pick AABB and be marked wrong. Distractor changed to AABA (32-bar song form).
findings.evidence: same lesson, n9 and n32; recomputation of the key against the options

findings.claim: “In the Eduqas GCSE Music exam (AoS1)…”
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md copyright and naming rules

findings.claim: “In the Eduqas composition briefs… composing a piece for an evening concert in ternary form for piano plus one other instrument.”
findings.truth: Names the board and reproduces a specimen composition brief. Replaced with a neutral sentence.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md copyright distancing; spec 2.2 (briefs are released to centres each September)

findings.claim: “If your Eduqas composition brief asks you to write in ternary form…”
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: “In the Eduqas listening exam…”
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the last question reads “8 marks (QWC assessed)”.
findings.truth: The appraising paper carries no quality-of-written-communication or SPaG allocation. The spec's assessment section lists 96 marks over eight questions and says nothing about written-communication marks.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3 and 3.1; no occurrence of SPaG, QWC or 'quality of written communication' anywhere in the spec

findings.claim: A general essay comparing binary and ternary form is labelled “12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)”.
findings.truth: No extract and no score are involved, so this is the wrong question type. It is an extended written response. The label also drives AI marking, which reads the first number in the type string as the total.
findings.evidence: js/main.js line 458 (marksMatch from q.type); scripts/pipeline_api_guides.py type_slugs enum

findings.claim: “Mozart’s Eine Kleine Nachtmusik (Third Movement) is a well-known example of rondo form.”
findings.truth: The third movement is the Menuetto, a minuet and trio, which is ternary. The rondo in that work is the second movement, the Romance in C major. Naming the wrong movement would cost the mark and teaches the opposite of the lesson's own binary/ternary test.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Eine kleine Nachtmusik (II Romance: Andante — rondo form; III Menuetto: Allegretto — minuet and trio)

findings.claim: “In the Eduqas GCSE listening exam, AoS1 questions…”
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: “Underline the structure of the Minuet, from which this extract is taken.”
findings.truth: A past-paper item keyed to a printed extract the student never receives, and to the minuet-and-trio set work that left this area of study when the Badinerie came in for summer 2022. Rewritten so it stands on its own; the answer is still ternary.
findings.evidence: docs/compliance-audit-past-papers.csv line 463 (Eduqas Sample/Practice Paper); spec p.13 (Badinerie is the prepared extract from summer 2022)

findings.claim: “you need to know six key devices” / “The six AoS1 musical devices are…”
findings.truth: The area of study lists about twenty devices: imitation, repetition, contrast, anacrusis, sequence, ostinato, syncopation, dotted rhythms, drone, pedal, canon, conjunct and disjunct movement, ornamentation, broken chord/arpeggio, alberti bass, regular phrasing, melodic and rhythmic motifs, chord progressions including cadences, and modulation. Presenting six as the complete examinable set is a scope error, and the same lesson goes on to teach several of the others.
findings.evidence: spec p.13, area of study 1 device list

findings.claim: “the free composition briefs for AoS1 specifically ask you to ‘make use of sequence’”
findings.truth: A free composition cannot carry a board brief. The brief for the first composition is set by the board and released to centres each September; for the second composition the learner writes the brief.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2, Component 2 composition briefs

findings.claim: “In the Eduqas GCSE Music specification for AoS1…” and “In the Eduqas listening exam…”
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: “Give a bar number during the extract where one example of the following musical features occurs: an ascending sequence”, labelled 12 marks, mark scheme worth 1 mark and ending “(This question is modelled on the Eduqas prepared extract format.)”
findings.truth: Three faults in one question: there is no extract, so it cannot be answered; the 12-mark label makes AI marking score a one-word answer out of 12; and the mark scheme names the board. Rewritten as a self-contained one-mark identification.
findings.evidence: js/main.js line 458; docs/compliance-audit-past-papers.csv line 462 (Eduqas Autumn 2020 Q1d)

findings.claim: Vivaldi's Winter: ascending sequences “during the second section to portray ‘biting, stinging winds.’”
findings.truth: The quotation has no source. Winter's first-movement sonnet reads “In the harsh breath of a horrid wind”. The sequence claim itself is sound, and Winter is in F minor as implied by nothing else on the page, so nothing is mis-taught; only the quotation marks are unearned.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, The Four Seasons (Vivaldi), Winter sonnet and translation

findings.claim: Domenico Alberti “(c.1710–1740)”.
findings.truth: Wikipedia gives c.1710 – 14 October 1746, noting 1740 as an alternative in some sources. Sources genuinely disagree, and the date is not examinable, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Domenico Alberti

findings.claim: Toto's Africa: “Riff b (bars 3–4)… five notes based on the E major pentatonic scale over a sustained chord ii (C♯m)… cut across the 2/2 time signature”.
findings.truth: Internally consistent (E major pentatonic and C sharp minor pentatonic are the same five notes, and C sharp minor is ii in B major, the verse key), but the bar numbers, the riff label and the 2/2 metre come from a set-work analysis that open sources do not confirm; Hooktheory reads the intro as C sharp minor i7. Not corrected because no true value was found. Africa is the popular-music prepared extract, not an AoS1 one.
findings.evidence: Hooktheory theorytab for Africa; Wikipedia, Africa (Toto song) carries no harmonic analysis

findings.claim: “The extract begins in F# minor. Other than B minor, name two keys to which the music modulates during Section B.”
findings.truth: The Badinerie begins in B minor. F sharp minor, the dominant minor, is where Section B begins. As printed, the question contradicted the lesson's own timeline and its knowledge check on the opening key.
findings.evidence: spec p.13 (Badinerie, Orchestral Suite No.2 in B minor); Wikipedia, Orchestral Suite No.2 (Bach); the verified free-tier listening deck at scripts/_content_music_listening_rebuild/b_badinerie_l3.py

findings.claim: “In the Eduqas listening exam, the Badinerie appears as a prepared extract with score worth 12 marks. You will be given the score and hear the extract three times.”
findings.truth: The spec sets no per-question tariff and no number of hearings. It does say scores must not be taken into the examination and that sections of the scores are printed on the paper when a question requires them. Board named as well.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3, Assessment of Component 3 (1 hour 15 minutes, 96 marks, eight questions, two on each area of study, scores not admitted)

findings.claim: “The rhythms are built from simple ostinato patterns…”
findings.truth: The Badinerie has no ostinato. The melodic device to name here is sequence; the rhythm is continuous quavers and semiquavers with repeated rhythmic cells. Writing “ostinato” about this movement in the exam would not be credited, and lesson 3 of this unit teaches the term precisely.
findings.evidence: scripts/_content_music_listening_rebuild/b_badinerie_l4.py (approved free-tier deck: melody built from scales, arpeggios and sequences; ostinato is used there only as a distractor)

findings.claim: Flashcard answer “1738ndash1739”, question “2 in B minor, composed in _____”.
findings.truth: The dash entity was stripped, leaving a nonsense answer, and the question is a truncated fragment. Answer is 1738–1739 (the partly autograph set of parts from Leipzig).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Orchestral Suite No.2 (Bach); recomputation of the card against the lesson text

findings.claim: After the two fixes above, 13 of the 24 practice questions still carry a type badge whose mark figure differs from their mark scheme total (for example 4-mark badge over a scheme capped at 2; lesson 2 question 2 is the reverse, a 1-mark badge over a 2-mark scheme).
findings.truth: Two readings are open. (a) The five type strings are a fixed taxonomy whose mark figure labels the CATEGORY, not the question, in which case nothing is wrong except the AI marker, and js/main.js should take the total from the mark scheme instead of the first number in q.type. (b) The figure is the question tariff, in which case 13 mark schemes need re-capping across this unit and the same fault will exist across every music unit. Recommendation: (a). Fix js/main.js and leave the schemes alone, because the taxonomy is generated from scripts/pipeline_api_guides.py and cannot be re-tariffed one unit at a time. This overlaps the 190 question-type relabels already queued in the retro programme.
findings.evidence: js/main.js line 458; scripts/pipeline_api_guides.py type_slugs

findings.claim: “The flute part has a two-octave pitch range.”
findings.truth: Plausible and widely repeated, but not verifiable without the score, which is not in the repo and not on an open page. Left alone.
findings.evidence: attempted verification against Wikipedia and the free-tier listening deck; neither states a range

findings.claim: Spec p.13 says “Learners must study the whole of Movement 3, including the trio” immediately above the Badinerie bullet.
findings.truth: Residue from the pre-2022 prepared extract, a minuet-and-trio third movement. The Badinerie is the seventh and final movement of the suite and has no trio. Nothing should ever be generated from that sentence.
findings.evidence: spec p.13 vs the Badinerie bullet (for assessment from summer 2022 onwards); Wikipedia, Orchestral Suite No.2 (Bach)

summary: Four HIGH errors: the minuet dated to the Classical era, Eine kleine Nachtmusik's third movement called a rondo, a Badinerie question claiming the movement begins in F sharp minor, and a one-mark question labelled 12 marks with no extract to answer it from. Nine places named the board to students. 25 edits across all four lessons; no lesson was clean.
